title: Introduction to the initiation and resolution of inflammation
why: The lecturer welcomes the students and outlines the lecture's focus on deepening existing knowledge of immune mechanisms.

title: Innate immune recognition of PAMPs and DAMPs
why: The lecturer introduces how the innate immune system senses infections directly through microbial products and indirectly through tissue damage.

title: Properties of effective PAMPs and self–non-self discrimination
why: The lecturer defines the necessary evolutionary criteria for pathogen-associated molecular patterns to distinguish self from non-self.

title: Germline encoding and cellular localisation of pattern recognition receptors
why: The lecturer explains that pattern recognition receptors are germline-encoded and positioned in specific cellular compartments to encounter pathogens.

title: Toll-like receptors and their microbial ligands
why: The lecturer describes the discovery, structure, and ligand specificity of Toll-like receptors, highlighting TLR4.

title: Location-dependent TLR signalling and synergy with cellular stress
why: The lecturer explains how surface and endosomal TLR signaling pathways lead to distinct gene responses and synergize with cellular stress.

title: Other pattern recognition receptor families and NOD2 in Crohn's disease
why: The lecturer introduces non-TLR pattern recognition receptors, focusing on cytoplasmic sensing and the role of NOD2 in Crohn's disease.

title: Inflammasome assembly, IL-1β activation and chronic inflammation
why: The lecturer details the structure of the inflammasome, its activation of caspase-1 and IL-1beta, and its triggering by non-infectious DAMPs.

title: Sentinel cell activation and local and systemic inflammatory effects
why: The lecturer explains how mast cells and macrophages respond to danger signals and produce both local and systemic inflammatory effects.

title: Leukocyte recruitment through adhesion, extravasation and chemotaxis
why: The lecturer details the multi-step mechanism of immune cell recruitment from blood vessels into inflamed tissues.

title: Lymphatic drainage and dendritic cell migration for adaptive immune priming
why: The lecturer describes how dendritic cells migrate through the lymphatic system to initiate adaptive immune responses in lymph nodes.

title: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
why: The lecturer discusses the dangerous clinical consequences when inflammatory cytokine production becomes excessive and systemic.

title: Passive and active mechanisms of inflammation resolution
why: The lecturer explains the mechanisms that terminate immune reactions, including mediator decay, lipid mediator switching, and anti-inflammatory cytokines.

title: Tissue repair and causes of persistent inflammation
why: The lecturer covers granulation tissue formation by fibroblasts and macrophages, and the factors leading to chronic inflammation and inflammaging.

title: Granuloma formation as a strategy for containing persistent infection
why: The lecturer explains how granuloma formation evolved as an adaptive response to wall off intractable pathogens like tuberculosis.

title: Lecture close: introduction to the next lecture on complement
why: The lecturer concludes the session and mentions the topic for the next lecture.
